name: FounderPal
tagline: A set of AI generators that spit out marketing strategy, personas, value props and landing page copy for solo founders.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: FounderPal is a collection of structured prompts wrapped in a clean form UI, sitting on top of a general purpose LLM. There is no proprietary model, no data network, and nothing that needs to phone home except the model API you already pay for. An agent can rebuild the generator pattern, input form, output panel, history, and copy-to-clipboard in one sitting. What you will not clone is the prompt craft: the templates are tuned by someone who has read a lot of marketing copy, and your first drafts will be blander until you tune yours. That is a tuning problem, not a build problem.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app with a menu of marketing generators that take a one-paragraph product description, run a curated prompt against an LLM API, and save every output to a local history you can re-run and edit.
requirements: An OpenAI or Anthropic API key with a small budget
Node 20 and a willingness to edit prompt templates by hand
Basic taste in marketing copy, since you are now the editor
whatYouLose: Prompt templates written by someone who does this for a living, which is most of the actual product
The breadth of generators, personas, value props, cold emails, ad copy, all pre-wired
Model and prompt updates when the underlying models change behaviour
Shareable hosted links and a polished UI you would not be embarrassed to show a cofounder
Any sense that the output was validated against real campaigns
moatNotes: The moat is prompt quality plus packaging. Both are copyable, one of them is just tedious.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because writing good prompts for positioning and copy is a skill, and paying once for someone else's tuned templates is cheaper than the three weeks you would spend discovering that your own prompt returns generic startup mush. The UI also removes the decision fatigue of a blank chat box: a form with labelled fields makes you actually finish the exercise. If you are already comfortable prompting an LLM directly, you are close to the finished product for free.
notes: This is a prompt library with good CSS, which is a real product and also a one-sitting build.
prompt:
Build a local-only web app called "MarketingBench": a personal collection of AI marketing generators.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Next.js 15 App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS
- SQLite via better-sqlite3 for history, file at ./data/bench.db
- Anthropic or OpenAI SDK, key read from .env.local as MODEL_API_KEY and MODEL_PROVIDER
- No auth, no accounts, no telemetry, no cloud database, runs on localhost only

Core model:
- A "generator" is defined in code as a TypeScript object in src/generators/: id, title, description, input fields (label, name, type text or textarea or select, placeholder, required), and a promptTemplate string using {{fieldName}} interpolation.
- Ship six generators seeded with real, opinionated prompts: marketing strategy outline, user persona, value proposition, landing page hero copy, cold email, and 10 social post hooks. Each prompt must demand specific, concrete output and explicitly ban generic startup filler.
- Generators are plain files so I can add and edit them without touching the app code.

UI:
- Home page: grid of generator cards.
- Generator page: form on the left from the field definitions, streamed output on the right rendered as markdown, plus copy button and regenerate button.
- History page: every run stored with generator id, inputs JSON, output text, model, timestamp. Clicking a run reloads its inputs into the form.
- A "project" concept: one saved product description in settings that auto-fills any field named product_description across all generators.

Out of scope: sharing links, multi-user, payments, image generation, analytics, deploy config.

Deliver: working app, npm run dev, .env.local.example, README with setup in under ten lines, and seed data so the history page is not empty on first run.
